subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is an algorithm?
options: A sequence of steps that can be followed to complete a task
A programming language used to build websites
A piece of computer hardware that stores data
A type of error found in computer programs
questions.explain: An algorithm is a set of well-defined, ordered steps for solving a problem or completing a task.

questions.q: In a flowchart, which symbol is used to represent a decision?
options: A diamond (rhombus)
A rectangle
A parallelogram
An oval (rounded rectangle)
questions.explain: A diamond represents a decision, where the flow branches depending on a yes/no or true/false condition.

questions.q: In a flowchart, which symbol represents an input or output?
options: A parallelogram
A diamond
A rectangle
An oval
questions.explain: A parallelogram is used for input and output operations in a flowchart.

questions.q: Why is pseudocode used to represent algorithms rather than a specific programming language?
options: It expresses the logic clearly without being tied to the syntax of any one language
It runs faster than real program code when executed
It is the only way computers can read an algorithm
It automatically fixes any errors in the logic
questions.explain: Pseudocode describes the steps of an algorithm in a readable way independent of a particular language's exact syntax.

questions.q: In a flowchart, which symbol is used for a process, such as a calculation or assignment?
options: A rectangle
A diamond
An oval
A parallelogram
questions.explain: A rectangle represents a process step such as a calculation or an assignment.

questions.q: What does the term 'decomposition' mean when designing algorithms?
options: Breaking a problem down into smaller, more manageable sub-problems
Removing all comments from the code
Converting pseudocode into machine code
Testing an algorithm with invalid data
questions.explain: Decomposition means breaking a complex problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve individually.

questions.q: The efficiency of an algorithm is most commonly measured by how much of which two resources it uses?
options: Time and memory (space)
Electricity and bandwidth
Storage and screen size
Colour and sound
questions.explain: Algorithm efficiency is usually judged by execution time and the amount of memory (space) used.

questions.q: Two different algorithms both correctly solve the same problem. Why might one still be preferred over the other?
options: One may be more efficient, completing the task in fewer steps or using less memory
A correct algorithm can never be improved upon
The longer algorithm is always the better choice
Efficiency has no effect on how a program performs
questions.explain: Even when two algorithms give correct results, the more efficient one uses fewer resources such as time or memory.

questions.q: Why does the efficiency of an algorithm become more important as the size of the input data increases?
options: The difference in the number of steps between algorithms grows larger with bigger inputs
Small inputs always take longer to process than large ones
Efficiency only matters for inputs of fewer than ten items
Larger inputs always require less memory
questions.explain: For large data sets, a less efficient algorithm's extra steps add up, making the performance gap much more significant.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how a linear search works?
options: It checks each item in the list one at a time from the start until the target is found
It repeatedly halves the list and discards one half each time
It sorts the list before searching every time
It only works on lists containing exactly a power of two items
questions.explain: A linear search inspects each element in turn until it finds the target or reaches the end of the list.

questions.q: What is a necessary precondition for a binary search to work correctly?
options: The list must already be sorted into order
The list must contain only whole numbers
The list must be empty
The list must be stored in reverse order only
questions.explain: A binary search relies on the data being in order so it can decide which half to discard at each step.

questions.q: Why is a binary search generally more efficient than a linear search on a large sorted list?
options: It roughly halves the number of remaining items to check at each step
It never has to compare any items
It examines every item twice to be certain
It only works when the target is the first item
questions.explain: By discarding half of the remaining items with each comparison, a binary search reaches the target far more quickly.

questions.q: You need to search an UNSORTED list of items for a particular value. Which search is appropriate?
options: A linear search
A binary search
A merge search
A bubble search
questions.explain: A binary search requires sorted data, so a linear search is the appropriate choice for an unsorted list.

questions.q: A binary search is used on the sorted list [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38] to find 23. Which item is examined first?
questions.explain: The middle item of a seven-element list is the fourth item, 12, which is examined first.

questions.q: How does a bubble sort put a list into order?
options: By repeatedly comparing adjacent items and swapping them if they are in the wrong order
By splitting the list in half repeatedly and merging the halves
By checking each item against the middle item only
By counting how many times each value appears
questions.explain: A bubble sort passes through the list comparing neighbouring pairs and swapping any that are out of order.

questions.q: Which technique does a merge sort use to sort a list?
options: Divide and conquer: repeatedly splitting the list then merging the parts in order
Comparing only adjacent items across a single pass
Searching for the largest item and deleting it
Randomly reordering items until they happen to be sorted
questions.explain: A merge sort divides the list into single-item sublists and then merges them back together in the correct order.

questions.q: For a large list of data, why is a merge sort usually preferred over a bubble sort?
options: A merge sort is generally more efficient, requiring fewer comparisons for large lists
A merge sort does not need to compare any items
A bubble sort cannot sort more than ten items
A merge sort always uses less memory than a bubble sort
questions.explain: Merge sort scales much better than bubble sort, so it is generally faster on large data sets.

questions.q: One complete pass of a bubble sort is performed on the list [5, 3, 8, 1]. What is the list after this first pass?
questions.explain: Swapping 5 and 3, leaving 5 and 8, then swapping 8 and 1 gives [3, 5, 1, 8], with the largest value at the end.

questions.q: Using a merge sort, the list [8, 3, 5, 1] is first split into single items and then merged. What is the result of merging the two sorted pairs [3, 8] and [1, 5]?
questions.explain: Merging the sorted pairs by repeatedly taking the smaller front item produces the fully sorted list [1, 3, 5, 8].

questions.q: In the worst case, a linear search on a list of n items examines how many items?
options: n items
1 item
n divided by 2 items
log of n items
questions.explain: In the worst case the target is last or absent, so a linear search must check all n items.

specSource: AQA GCSE Computer Science (8525) specification; Fundamentals Of Algorithms
